newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU assessment, country-by-country, of new members.
newsitem.headline: EU assessment, country-by-country, of new members.

text.p: Following are the main reasons given by the European Commission on Wednesday for recommending Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovenia, Estonia and Cyprus as ready for EU entry talks early next year.
The EU executive's central argument is that they are all democratic countries with stable institutions and functioning market economies.
POLAND
With a population of 38.6 million, Poland, which applied for EU membership in 1994, is the biggest and most heavily populated candidate country.

With its gross domestic product (GDP) per head standing at 31 percent of the EU average, Poland is seen as capable of standing up in the medium term to the increased competition membership will bring if it continues its reforms.

But the Commission insists bigger efforts are needed to achieve long-term stabilisation via reform of its retirement and social security systems and its banking sector. Big investments are also needed in the area of transport and the environment and more needs to be done to restructure state-owned enterprises.
One of Poland's biggest challenges will be to modernise its agriculture sector, which employs 27 percent of the active population and accounts for 6.6 percent of national production.
THE CZECH REPUBLIC

With a population of 10.3 million, a GDP per head at 55 percent the EU average and one of the lowest unemployment rates in a European market economy, the Czech Republic, which applied for EU membership in 1996, has made enormous progress, the Commission says. But extra reforms will be needed.
Recent disturbances show that more needs to be done to control the financial system, the Commission says.
As long as the Czech Republic speeds up the restructuring of its business sector it should be capable in the medium term of meeting the increased competition of EU membership, it says.
HUNGARY

One of the bright stars in the eyes of the Commission, Hungary is seen as having successfully transposed the EU's laws in preparation for membership. It is judged well-placed to match up to competition in the medium term if it continues its efforts.

Nevertheless, there are problems. The 10.2 million Hungarians have a GDP per head equal to only 37 percent of the EU average. After GDP fell nearly 20 percent between 1989 and 1993, the economy has started to grow, albeit at a weak pace, the Commission says.
There are also large problems in the area of the environment, it says.
SLOVENIA

With a GDP per head standing at 59 percent of the EU average, Slovenia is the richest of the candidate countries. The former Yugoslav republic of two million people, which applied for EU membership in June 1996, has a functioning market economy which has been largely privatised and is seen as capable in the medium term of supporting the extra competition brought by EU membership, the Commission says.

But it highlights some problems. The country's rigid system, whereby economic decisions are taken by consensus, needs to be loosened. The restructuring of companies has been slow, while large salary increases have reduced competitiveness and the management of the environment leaves something to be desired.
ESTONIA

Estonia has received the best marks from the Commission out of the three Baltic states. With 1.5 million inhabitants, Estonia is a poor country, with a GDP per head of only 23 percent of the EU average. But its economic reforms have won the Commission's favour. These include liberalisation of its external trade system and privatisation of the public sector. But the country needs to do more to face up to competitive pressure, the Commission said, calling the rise in its trade deficit as worrying.
CYPRUS

This Mediterranean island of 700,000 people, divided between Greek and Turkish communities, is a special case and its membership application, submitted in 1990, was judged on different criteria from the five eastern European candidates.
EU leaders decided in 1995 that talks with Cyprus should start six months after the end of the EU's inter-governmental conference on treaty reforms, which wound up in Amsterdam on June 16-17.

The Commission said in 1993 it believed the perspective of EU membership would give an incentive to the island's two communities to reach a peace agreement. At the same time, the division remains the main obstacle to the island's EU membership.

Cyprus faces few economic problems, even though the northern third, occupied by Turkish troops, is notably poorer, as the south gains its prosperity from tourism. The EU says this gulf will be easier to bridge if the island joins the EU.
